results.summary:
Misconfigured databases remain the leading cause of global data breaches, exposing millions of sensitive records due to human error, inadequate security settings, and neglected backup file management.

### Key Points
- Misconfigured databases often lack basic password protection, use default credentials, or disable security logs, making them easily discoverable on the public internet.
- Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler recently identified four unprotected databases linked to the Tribeca Film Festival, exposing over 666,000 records including personal contact information.
- Major historical incidents include the 2017 exposure of 1.1 TB of Republican National Committee voter data and the 2020 leak of 243 million Brazilian health records.
- Backup files, archives, and development environments are frequently overlooked, serving as high-value targets for cybercriminals seeking concentrated sensitive data.
- Under the shared responsibility model, cloud providers secure the infrastructure, but customers are solely responsible for configuring firewalls and applying security patches to their own data.

### Why it Matters
These preventable security lapses create long-term risks for individuals, including identity theft, financial fraud, and targeted social engineering scams. For organizations, the failure to secure databases leads to severe reputational damage, regulatory fines, and significant operational disruption.

results.title: Gears of War: E-Day's new Horde may be the game's most interesting mode, but it left me with more questions than answers
results.author: Sherif Saed
results.content:
I've been eager to get my hands on Gears of War: E-Day's new Horde mode, Horde Siege, which appears to be a more smartly designed, more engaging iteration. June's Xbox bonanza first look sold me on the campaign, but the iconic mode has long been my favourite non-campaign mode in Gears. And at least so far - looks to be the most revolutionary Horde ever.
Before I get into my time with it, I have to add a caveat: this hasn't been the most organised preview event I've taken part in. Account authentication and build encryption issues - on two separate occasions - prevented me from delving as deep into it as I could. All told, I only got to play for a little over two hours.
This might be circumstantial, but it's worth noting Xbox recently cut thousands of jobs, and it's hard to imagine how that wouldn't affect the integrity of similar events. This isn't Xbox's first digital preview; I've been to several over the years, including for the Gears of War series, and I can't think of anything that comes close to last week's E-Day event.
My biggest takeaway from playing Horde Siege is that it feels like a standalone game that could easily exist outside E-Day. Classic Horde - i.e., surviving a set number of waves in a small area - always felt like clever re-use of assets. Siege is an evolution that builds on that legacy to offer something entirely new, particularly to those who could never get into Horde.
Siege matches take place in an open world, of a sort: a sprawling (by Gears standards) map with multiple objectives. You start off in one corner with your four-player squad, and immediately receive an objective that sends you to a different area. Your main goal typically revolves around a data-collecting device called the R.I.G. Sometimes you need to lure out Locust to "recalibrate it", other times you're tasked with defending it.
Siege maps, meanwhile, make excellent use of their size by dotting secondary objectives around their many sections. I've seen enough variety in my limited time to make me excited to tackle all of them in the final build.
There's a push for quiet exploration in Siege - a stark contrast to classic Horde's unrelenting onslaughts - underpinned by those secondary objectives. Outside of creating excuses for you to visit areas you may otherwise ignore, they are integral to the flow of gameplay. For one, clearing them awards Squad Perks, in-match stat-boosting modifiers. At the risk of causing you to click off this page, the closest approximation I can think of is, well, MOBAs. Like them, the flow of Siege encourages clearing multiple side objectives to get your character strong enough to tackle bosses and future waves.
What caught me completely off-guard, though, was a slight extraction shooter element: another reward for completing side objectives are Weapon Parts. Unlike Squad Perks, however, they're entirely useless within the round itself. If you successfully extract with your parts intact (no pun intended), you can later use them to upgrade your weapons.
Yes, extraction is now a core Horde mechanic. It immediately reminded me of the recent iterations of Zombies in Call of Duty, where you get the choice of extracting and keeping your XP every 10 or so waves. It works similarly here, and it's your only way out. The rush I felt in those three-minute holdouts as everyone waits for the helicopter, fending off wave after wave of Locust, is remarkably similar to late-round extractions in Zombies.
There's an emphasis on scale here that takes advantage of the large maps. While your immediate concern is your squad, there are three other squads that start at different parts of the map, each tackling their own objectives. It's common to cross paths with them, and you can certainly help each other, but the real reason three squads are even in the same match is Boss Invasions, which more deliberately bring everyone together against a common - very large - enemy.
These Boss Invasions were another highlight, particularly at the start as everyone pours in to take down the invading boss, whose scale is on the level of major spectacle moments from Gears campaigns. Invasions turn Horde from an intimate test of skill for four players to something akin to Destiny's Public Events.
My most played mode in the preview, meanwhile, was the aptly named Blitz; a truncated version of Horde that plays out like a speedrun of Siege. Blitz rounds take around 15-20 minutes to complete. Each match picks different objectives from Siege proper to create a condensed version of the real deal, which is part of what made it easy to pick up and enjoy. Blitz exists to offer a straight-to-the-point variant of Siege for those short on time, but it's a complete experience on its own that you wouldn't guess is the smaller sibling of a bigger mode.
Horde Siege evidently has plenty to chew on, even if preview event logistics put a damper on my first impression. I can tell I'm going to be spending a lot of time with it.

- Xbox admits its game exclusivity strategy isn't "obvious", but insists Gears of War and Clockwork Revolution won't be the only non-PlayStation games
- Microsoft is reportedly considering making more of its first-party games exclusive to Xbox
- Microsoft announces 3200 layoffs and four studio departures in "most significant" Xbox restructuring in history
results.summary:
Gears of War: E-Day introduces Horde Siege, a revolutionary new mode featuring open-world objectives, extraction mechanics, and large-scale boss battles that significantly evolve the classic survival gameplay.

### Key Points
- Horde Siege replaces traditional wave-based survival with a sprawling map featuring dynamic objectives and a four-player squad structure.
- The mode incorporates MOBA-inspired Squad Perks and extraction shooter elements, allowing players to secure Weapon Parts for permanent upgrades.
- Boss Invasions bring multiple squads together for large-scale combat encounters similar to public events in other live-service titles.
- A condensed version of the mode, called Blitz, offers a faster, 15-to-20-minute gameplay experience for players with limited time.
- Technical issues and logistical challenges during the preview event hindered the initial testing process for some participants.

### Why it Matters
This evolution of the iconic Horde mode signals a major shift in the Gears of War franchise toward more complex, objective-driven multiplayer experiences. By integrating extraction and progression mechanics, Microsoft is positioning the series to compete with modern live-service shooters and broaden its appeal to a wider audience.

results.title: Baby Busts and GDP Booms: Demographic Change and the Macroeconomy
results.author: Yves Smith
results.content:
Yves here. In the dry realm of macroeconomics, this study presents cheery news. It’s taken as a truism that an aging population, aka demographic decline, is a death kneel to economic growth. The assumption has been that the dependency ratio, as in the proportion of workers compared to those not engaged in deemed-to-be-productive activity, as in children and oldsters, is fundamental to increasing output. Can’t have too many useless eaters!
This article documents what many have argued: that technology can offset the perceived drag of having an increasing level of the population not engaging in paid employment.
By Daron Acemoglu, Institute Professor in the Department of Economics Massachusetts Institute of Technology; David Autor, Ford Professor of Economics Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Keelan Beirne, PhD candidate in Economics Massachusetts Institute of Technology; and Andrew Scott, Senior Director of Economics Ellison Institute Of Technology, Oxford; Professor of Economics London Business School. Originally published at VoxEU
Globally declining birth rates have, over the last seven decades, slowed population growth and raised average ages. This column argues that despite widespread economic pessimism, historical cross-country and US commuting zone data point to no impact of ageing populations on aggregate GDP or earnings growth. Countries with lower birth rates have higher GDP growth per working-age adult, and US commuting zones with lower birth rates have faster wage growth. The growth-reducing potential of demographic slowdowns is countered by faster technological change. While future demographic changes will occur at greater speed and scale, the economic record suggests that current pessimism is premature.
Editors’ note: This column is based on CEPR Discussion Paper 21673 “Baby busts and growth booms: Demographic change and the macroeconomy”.
Over the past seven decades, birth rates have declined sharply across the globe, as seen in Figure 1. In 1950, the global average number of births per 100 people (the ‘crude birth rate’) was 3.78. By 2025, it had more than halved to 1.71. As a consequence, the United Nations forecasts an absolute fall in the global human population in the second half of the 21st century, the first sustained drop since the bubonic plague of the 14th century. The countries with the lowest birth rates today – China at 0.63, Japan at 0.60, and the Republic of Korea at 0.46 – are projected by 2050 to see their populations decline by 20–30%, their share of the population aged 65+ reach 30–40%, and their older working populations (45+) come to encompass 60% of their workforces.
Figure 1 Global trends in birth rates
Source: UN Population Prospects 2024.
These demographic trends are a source of widespread concern to economists and policymakers. Older workers are widely assumed to be less productive, less innovative, less entrepreneurial, and less technologically adept than younger adults. Accounting for these factors, long-term scenario analyses project slowing economic growth (e.g. IMF 2025, OECD 2025, Coelli et al. 2025) and worsening public finances (e.g. Cooley et al. 2024, Favero and Srivastava 2025).
These concerns rest largely on forward projections. But the global economy has already experienced sharp demographic changes over the past decades. This historical evidence can attest to whether this widespread pessimism concerning the impact of ageing and declining populations is warranted.
That is the exercise we undertake in Acemoglu et al. (2026), in which we study two complementary sources of evidence. The first is from cross-country variation in the timing and extent of birth rate fluctuations. The sample includes all countries with populations over 1 million, excluding tax havens and crisis-affected states, and covers the period 1950 to 2020. The second is regional US variation across 722 commuting zones covering the contiguous US, with the workforce partitioned into ‘younger’ (aged 20–45) and ‘older’ (aged 45–70) adults.
To isolate exogenous variation in fertility (that is not caused by contemporaneous or future anticipated economic conditions), the key variable of focus is birth rates from decades earlier. These affect current populations but are not caused by current conditions. For instance, the 1950 birth rate is used as a source of variation for analysing the impact of declining fertility on GDP and wage growth between 1970 and 2020.
Figure 2 documents the central findings from analysis of cross-national and cross-US-regional data: countries with lower birth rates have higher growth in GDP per working-age adult, and commuting zones with lower birth rates experience faster average wage growth. There is no evidence of significant impact from lower birth rates on aggregate GDP growth or aggregate earnings – meaning that the increases in per capita GDP and wage growth associated with falling birth rates are sufficient to offset any decline in population. The cross-country magnitude of this effect from falling birth rates is economically (as well as statistically) significant: a one-percentage-point lower birth rate is associated with an approximately 22% higher GDP per worker 40 years later and 29% after 60 years.
Figure 2 Birth rates and growth
Notes: This figure reports event study estimates of the impact of birth rates on income growth across countries and US commuting zones, allowing for initial income and population share of younger and older adults. See Acemoglu et al. (2026) for details.
The positive impact on growth in GDP per working-age adult and average wages combined with no overall impact on growth in GDP or aggregate earnings is inconsistent with canonical models of economic growth. The standard Solow/Neoclassical growth model predicts an initial increase in GDP per worker that dissipates as the capital stock adjusts, and unambiguously predicts a decline in GDP – neither of which is supported by our results.
These estimates account for many factors expected to impact GDP and wage growth, including initial income and wages and initial demographic structure. Additionally, we drill down on several leading candidate explanations. Falling birth rates could raise growth by drawing more women into the formal workforce; by shifting child-rearing from ‘quantity’ to ‘quality’, with greater human capital investment per child; or by reallocating workers from low-productivity agriculture into higher-productivity manufacturing. For each of these channels, we find no consistent support in either cross-country or across commuting zone data. This, and the long lasting nature of our result across multiple decades (Kotschy and Bloom 2023), suggests our results are distinct from previous results articulating a ‘demographic dividend’.
Instead, the economic origin of the positive association between low birth rates and rising GDP per worker appears to be technological change that is itself induced by labour scarcity. Countries with the largest declines in fertility experience the largest shifts toward high-tech exports and high-tech employment. Similarly, in US commuting zones, lower birth rates spur an employment shift toward R&D intensive industries and an increase in labour-saving patenting (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Response of employment across commuting zones
Notes: This figure reports event study estimates of the impact of birth rates on employment composition across US commuting zones. See Acemoglu et al. (2026) for details.
Because lower birth rates simultaneously reduce population growth and raise the share of older people, our primary results are silent on the relative importance of population decline versus population ageing. Wars offer a grim natural experiment for separating the two. WWII casualties allow us to distinguish the economic effects of civilian deaths (which primarily reduce population without changing the age structure) from military deaths (which both reduce population and raise the average age of the workforce).
Figure 4 shows that total war deaths are associated with lower future GDP per worker, while military deaths predict higher GDP per worker, suggesting that it is the scarcity of younger workers that induces the positive productivity response. This pattern parallels Bergeaud et al. (2025), who document that French regions with higher WWI military mortality experienced increased patenting in labour-saving technologies.
Figure 4 Response of GDP to WWII deaths
Notes: This figure reports event study estimates of the impact of WWII death rates on future GDP growth across countries. See Acemoglu et al. (2026) for details.
These findings build on earlier work documenting that changes in the ratio of older to younger workers stimulate the development and adoption of labour-saving technologies (Acemoglu 2010, Acemoglu and Restrepo 2017). To our knowledge, however, no prior research documents the striking long-run increase in income per worker that accompanies falling birth rates.
Seven decades of macroeconomic and demographic data do not support the conventional view, hard-baked into much economic analysis of demographic change, that slowing fertility means falling living standards. We cannot however rule out that the decades ahead could confirm the conventional wisdom that evidence so far fails to support. One key source of uncertainty is that countries will experience demographic changes at a speed and magnitude rarely seen in historical data. China, for instance, is expected to see its population aged 15 to 64 years decline from a peak of 1 billion to around 300 million by 2100.
Perhaps not by coincidence, China is also far ahead of other nations in its development and adoption of robotics. China’s count of industrial robots doubled between 2021 and 2024 and now accounts for nearly 50% of the global stock (Financial Times 2026). That suggests that the channel of directed technological change is very much at work, but it remains an open question whether, given the scale of China’s demographic challenge, this will be sufficient to stabilise GDP growth in the manner our results indicate has happened over the last several decades.
Additionally, the dramatic demographic changes currently underway are co-occurring with rising life expectancy (Scott 2021, 2024), which may itself spur institutional changes, policies, and additional human capital investments that complement longer lifespans.
While our demographic futures are relatively assured, our economic possibilities are still uncertain and will evolve according to technological and human investments, including in the field of artificial intelligence. Based on the last seven decades, it is these reactions that will determine our economic future.
See original post for references
results.summary:
New research from MIT and London Business School economists suggests that declining birth rates do not necessarily hinder economic growth, as technological innovation effectively offsets demographic workforce challenges.

### Key Points
- Historical data from 1950 to 2020 shows no evidence that aging populations reduce aggregate GDP or earnings growth.
- Countries and US regions with lower birth rates demonstrate higher GDP growth per working-age adult and faster wage increases.
- Labor scarcity caused by demographic shifts incentivizes the development and adoption of labor-saving technologies and R&D-intensive industries.
- Analysis of WWII casualty data indicates that a scarcity of younger workers specifically drives positive productivity responses through technological adaptation.
- China’s rapid adoption of industrial robotics serves as a modern example of economies responding to significant demographic decline through automation.

### Why it Matters
These findings challenge the long-standing economic consensus that aging populations inevitably lead to stagnation and declining living standards. By highlighting the role of technological innovation as a compensatory mechanism, the study suggests that future economic prosperity depends more on human and technological investment than on demographic trends alone.

results.title: Home Invasions
results.source: The New York Review of Books
results.author: Laura Marsh
results.content:
John Lanchester is so adept at explaining political and economic catastrophes that it is easy to forget he has written six novels and a collection of tech-infused ghost stories. His capacious essays—on the global financial crisis, Greek debt, Brexit, the pandemic—have an almost soothing quality, as he sketches out the underlying questions, glosses technical terms, and calmly conveys how bad things might be. “The story of Northern Rock was a fuck-up,” he wrote in the London Review of Books in January 2008, a few months after the British bank collapsed and half a year before Lehman Brothers fell. “The trouble is that it may turn out to be a harbinger of meltdown too.” This is typical Lanchester: easygoing, but blunt; colloquial, but precise; deeply informed, yet detached, even placid. He doesn’t argue so much as observe. “It’s going to be interesting—to put it very, very mildly,” he wrote in October 2008, mid-meltdown, “to see if the bail-out works.”
His most celebrated novel, Capital (2012), shares some of the appealing features of his essays. While the novel is richly populated with distinctive characters—ranging from the insufferable, genteel banker Roger Yount to his sociopathic deputy Mark to a Senegalese soccer prodigy to a Zimbabwean meter maid awaiting her asylum hearing—it proceeds methodically, like a work of journalism. It makes the most of Lanchester’s powers of explication, slowly presenting the pieces of its central puzzle. (In this case: Who has been sending disturbing postcards to each resident of one very expensive street in London?) And like many of his LRB articles and two of his nonfiction books, How to Speak Money (2014) and IOU : Why Everyone Owes Everyone and No One Can Pay (2010), it revolves around finance, as it traces how capital inflates and punctures the hopes of ordinary people who are making art, falling in love, getting arrested, getting divorced, getting deported, or dying in the months leading up to the 2008 crash.
Capital was a doorstopper work of realism—an examination of a knowable, mostly rational world (albeit one on the brink of implosion). Lanchester’s subsequent fiction has departed sharply from that mode, incorporating the increasingly eerie features of tech and the intrusion of irrational politics into our lives. The Wall (2019) is a pared-back dystopia in which citizens of a paranoid xenophobic state are periodically pressed into service as border guards. Political euphemisms abound, initiative is forbidden, the rule of the land is unquestioned authority—a society whose brutality is all on the surface, without subtexts to parse.* The short stories in Reality (2020) feel warmer: many of them thrum with the cozy rhythms of middle-class life (children asking parents how soon they can request the Wi-Fi password when visiting a family friend’s house; an academic grousing about the caliber of papers at an obscure conference), until a shiver of the unexplained intrudes. The characters are undone in part by supernatural disturbances, and in part by their life-sapping obsessions with their phones (“Cold Call,” “Signal”), with themselves as reflected in their phones (the death-portending selfies of “Charity”), or with soul-sucking reality TV (the title story, “Reality,” which originally ran in the LRB as “Love Island”). Behavior that passes for normal in the twenty-first century in fact leads us on a descent into hell.
His new book, Look What You Made Me Do, falls somewhere between Capital and Reality: it begins like a conventional realist novel, a beautifully observed portrait of a marriage shattered by grief and infidelity, with subtle, original things to say about those timeless ordeals. But less than halfway through it turns into something more sensational and disorienting. A series of plot twists whisks us into the realm of Black Mirror. A smart-home hack, a hit Netflix show that uncannily resembles real life, and a crypto fraud subplot—these nightmarish turns are presented not as self-conscious excursions into the Twilight Zone, as the stories in Reality are, but as a plausible continuation of events. And though they might not always land gracefully, they evoke quite accurately a tech-poisoned form of cracking up. This could have been a novel solely about the private world of a middle-aged couple; instead, Lanchester is more interested in how privacy can be distorted and deranged, obliterated or weaponized, at the click of a button.
Kate and Jack Hittlestone are a perfectly nice middle-class couple who are also acutely aware that if their friends could hear the way they spoke behind closed doors, they might lose a few of them. “Every successful marriage has its own private language,” Kate, the narrator, muses in the opening line. A couple’s lexicon of running jokes, catchphrases, and allusions would at best make little sense to outsiders; at worst, they’d sound “cruel, or mean spirited, or at the very least unfair and inappropriate.” To Jack, Kate’s friends are “the hags” and “the enormous great big hairy lesbians”; he jokes that their neighbor, “the Poisoner,” killed her ex and buried him under the patio. The way the couple talks about sex is equally colorful and mystifying. “Christmas Eve and Ho Chi Minh’s birthday” do not sound all that kinky, but these are the special occasions on which the Hittlestones hire an escort to have sex with Kate while Jack watches. Meanwhile, one of Jack’s favorite expressions—“Want your body, disco doll”—does not mean he is horny; it’s something he says when they’re running late and he needs Kate to come downstairs so they can leave.
Advertisement
That these private things remain private is essential not only to the Hittlestones’ marriage but also to their social standing. Jack is an architect who earns so much that Kate has quit her job teaching art history and devotes herself to volunteer work, counseling prisoners. The friends they visit in the first chapter are also architects, whose impeccably renovated town house has swallowed the one next door, showing an extreme commitment to the craze for knocking through walls and opening up floor plans. There are deliciously petty distinctions in class and taste among these well-to-do Londoners. The friends’ house is a little too neat and camera ready, Kate thinks: “It’s not Hello! vulgar, but on the other hand it is Architectural Digest vulgar.”
Still, Kate is a better-than-average guest, a peaceable, likable person who wryly accepts the responsibility to keep conversation going over dinner. Sensing a lull, she provides a series of polite questions that allow the other guests to talk endlessly about themselves. “What I really wanted to do was sit there in silence and wait for someone to ask me a question, show some interest, engage with me, see me,” she thinks. “What I did instead, with a heavy internal sigh, was turn to the TV person and say: ‘Have you ever done a cooking show?’” You get the sense that when she enjoys a mean thought or two about her hosts, she is simply giving herself a short break from the thankless social obligations that come with being a basically nice woman in her fifties.
Obligations have little hold over Jack. He treats the other guests as his audience and doesn’t hesitate to try out his most provocative material on them: a diatribe about people who cook Yotam Ottolenghi recipes for dinner parties (“You see the pomegranate seeds strewn all over everything and you know what’s coming”), and those who pretend to like it (“And everybody says ooh yummy Ottolenghi”), clearly desperate for someone to take offense. For Kate, there’s something familiar and comforting about these mildly abrasive social commentaries, and they’re also a large part of the novel’s appeal, as they needle the reader’s narrow cultural preferences. (Who among us has not attempted Plenty?) When Kate first laid eyes on Jack, in a college bar at Oxford, he was doing a similar bit, riffing on the name “Virgin” airlines and claiming that he’d like to start a company with the even more out-there name “Anal Sex.” A speech that some might find tiresome Kate found irresistible.
So a sense of the scale and complexity of her loss is clear when Jack dies suddenly, even though she can say little about her grief itself. Kate professes that she has undergone a period of dissociation in the months after her husband’s death, insisting that for her the phrase “I don’t know how I got through it” is literally true, and that she retains no memory of the early stages of bereavement. Though she expected grief to manifest as “a terrible roaring…from the air,” Kate feels only an intense absence, Jack’s “not there-ness, the hole where my life had been.” No more in-jokes, no more Ho Chi Minh’s birthday, no more doting on the parts of Jack’s character that everyone else could do without. It is a desolation like that Siri Hustvedt describes in Ghost Stories, her recent memoir of the loss of her husband, Paul Auster: “I am mourning Siri and Paul. I am mourning AND. I am mourning how the AND made me feel in the world.”
Yet Kate’s loss mutates into something more unstable, potent, and singular when she hears of a new Netflix show called Cheating, which portrays a man exactly like Jack, who uses their own private language in intimate scenes with a young woman, and reveals to the other woman the deepest secrets of a marriage exactly like Jack and Kate’s. The only explanation Kate can think of is that shortly before he died, Jack had an affair with the writer of the show, and the writer turned it all into material. She had trusted that these were “the things we kept entirely for each other. Our private space. But it turned out that this was just Jack’s way of carrying on, and he was as capable of doing it with another woman as he was with me.” Her husband was not the man she thought he was, a sickening realization that prevents her from mourning and finding a way to go on. How do you grieve when you do not know the person you are grieving?
Advertisement
Cheating is a violation of Kate’s privacy, but not in the way she thinks. An affair is an individual betrayal. But as Kate comes to discover, the showrunner—an up-and-coming writer named Phoebe Mull, a woman they barely knew—did not gather Kate’s deepest secrets by sleeping with Jack. A far more pervasive and impersonal network of surveillance allowed Phoebe to listen in on Jack and Kate chatting away to each other inside their home. She simply hacked their smart home (gaining access to everything that was said there, thanks to the system’s voice activation) and then refashioned their conversations into saucy dialogue for Jerry, his mistress, Tina, and his oblivious wife, Charlotte. Why subject the Hittlestones in particular to this treatment? It would spoil the layers of mystery Lanchester builds around this relationship to say more than that long ago they opened a wound Phoebe is still tending. Her revenge is to produce a TV show that will make Kate suspect infidelity and wreck her marriage, which might have worked if Jack hadn’t died before the show aired.
Nonetheless, she succeeds in torturing Kate. A weakness of the novel is that Kate never seems to register any relief once she realizes that her beloved Jack was in fact faithful to the end. She is too consumed with the rage and humiliation of seeing her life twisted and turned into cheap entertainment. The novel alternates between Kate’s first-person narrative and Phoebe’s, with excerpts from the Cheating screenplay and other interludes here and there. Lanchester delights in the thinness of Phoebe’s script, the plunk with which Jerry’s “want your body, disco doll” lands during an assignation with Tina, who spits back, “Is that one of the things you say to her? One of your lines?” Even Jack’s Ottolenghi bit is overdone in Cheating, whose stage directions tell us that Jerry “looks at the cookbooks on display. He picks one up for Charlotte’s inspections.” Guess what? “It’s by Ottolenghi.”
The hype around Cheating—the “one TV show that everyone’s consuming at the same time”—means that Kate’s friends unknowingly join in trampling all over her private life. Ads for the show are appearing on billboards and the sides of buses. Phoebe may be guilty of a gross invasion of privacy, but there’s also a sense in which the public is complicit for bingeing on this kind of dreck, and flattering it and themselves by pretending it’s a form of art. You can guess exactly where Cheating sits in the streaming pantheon by the way people in the novel ask each other, “Do you think Cheating is better than Succession, White Lotus… Sopranos?” (It’s not.)
Phoebe’s attack on Kate is just one piece of a bigger assault on private life, namely the way that technology has eroded long-standing distinctions between personal, often intimate spaces and the public sphere. As Kate reflects, “Perhaps the boundaries between people are more porous today, since we have full access to all the information known to humanity, everywhere, all the time; we blur into the world around us and our stories leak out too.” And isn’t this also Jack’s fault, for delegating so many of his daily tasks to a computer? Kate thinks Jack’s habit of asking his weather app if it’s raining outside, instead of looking out the window, is cute; ditto his delight in their home’s voice-controlled appliances. In retrospect, the price turned out to be a tech company recording their every utterance every day.
Though Phoebe has little compunction about raiding Kate’s life, she tries not to reveal too much of her own, aware that a voyeuristic public will devour any scrap of scandal around a semifamous writer, an easy target. One of the most fun passages in Look What You Made Me Do is a complete chapter written with spiky flair as a newspaper profile of Phoebe, of the sort that Decca Aitkenhead used to write for The Guardian. A huge reason for the success of Cheating, as the profile makes clear, is that people assume Phoebe is laying bare her own sexual history in the show, that she—“author of this summer’s most talked-about TV, a steamy, sexy, bitter, nasty, devastating piece full of self-confessedly autobiographical detail”—must be the show’s Other Woman character, Tina. After snooping through Phoebe’s fridge and assessing the hotness of her boyfriend, Tony, the interviewer decides the conversation is too friendly and tries to inject some tension by taunting her, “You’re not very nice, are you?”
Phoebe’s defense mechanism involves acting as if she doesn’t care what people think. Her agent advises her to present an edgy persona to the world: “dark,” “fascinated by amorality,” “the other side of cancellation and virtue signalling.” At the heart of her act, however, lies a deeply conventional sense of what should be kept private, what is sacrosanct. This isn’t lost on the newspaper interviewer, who calls Phoebe an example of “that modern kind of candour, a woman who is willing to talk at length about sex and money but won’t say a word about more private subjects such as family or love.” The sections Phoebe narrates are a little flat compared with Kate’s, in part because her concerns are more mundane: she is a striver, touchy about success and the pressure to produce more of it, touchy around her difficult mother and absentee twin brother, and later (rightly) touchy when she becomes the target of a campaign of online and then offline harassment.
The alternating voices work well to contrast each woman’s point of view. Phoebe’s self-fashioning as a star TV writer, in “a scallop-topped pink shirt and red Izzy Marant trousers,” is undercut when Kate describes her as “gobby and over-made-up, with dyed red hair.” And the alternation between Phoebe, Kate, screenplay, and profile works to create an impression of everyone’s business being made too widely available to everyone else. There is no omniscient narrator here who has sole custody of the plot, as in Capital. Phoebe and Kate both know their own story and more than they should know about others’ too. They cannot stop oversharing and in the process “telling on themselves,” as social media parlance would have it.
Streaming, surveillance, and the Internet more broadly have reshaped the rhythms of entertainment and social life for most people, whether they’re enthusiastic about them or not. The consequences, when negative, are often insidious; a small convenience or guilty pleasure becomes a barrier to authentic connection with actual humans in real life, and so on. Crypto, however, is a niche pursuit—in the UK, only about 8 percent of people own cryptocurrency—and is often used in deliberately criminal enterprises, a subject Lanchester has written about several times in the LRB.
In the novel’s final third Kate gets her revenge on Phoebe through crypto, framing her boyfriend, Tony, for a heist and setting him up for a harrowing criminal trial. There’s a strong symmetry in this conclusion: Phoebe used her streaming show to create a fake secret life for Jack; now Kate has created a fake online life for Tony and planted it on his computer. Yet the act of framing someone for a crime is far-fetched, to say the least, and so logistically and technically complicated that it makes for a strange departure from the story of two women locked in psychological warfare.
The hardest thing to believe is that Kate is sadistic enough to inflict such a brutal punishment on anyone, let alone Tony, who was completely innocent of Phoebe’s Cheating scheme. This is conscientious and empathetic Kate, who wondered to herself, at the architects’ dinner party,
if any men ever feel that they are picking up the burden of social obligation like a huge bag of other people’s laundry; laundry that you don’t want to do, that in an ideal world you wouldn’t have to do, and yet that in this world, somehow, without your ever having volunteered for the task, is your responsibility.
Maybe her treatment of Tony is a punishment that one might idly fantasize about inflicting, or make threats about from the safety of an anonymous social media account, full of anger and self-righteousness. But it’s hard to believe that, even after the psychic rupture of losing her husband, this character would develop the deviousness and lack of remorse required to jeopardize an innocent person’s freedom.
This ending, with its disregard for innocence and guilt, reminded me of “Which of These Would You Like?,” the most stylized, almost fable-like story from Reality. The unnamed narrator is a prisoner in an unnamed country, possibly a state that does not yet exist, in some dystopian future. He does not know what his offense was, and the guards won’t tell him. Every day they ask him to choose a number of items from a brochure—which mask would he like, which gown, which cuffs, which scaffold—until you realize he is being asked to choose the manner of his own execution, daily, until the actual day arrives. He can decide how much resistance to show during this ritual, but he cannot change his fate.
By the end of Look What You Made Me Do, Kate resembles one of the guards in the story. She has resumed her volunteer work as a prison visitor after a bereavement leave, and she visits Tony, not to help him but to enjoy seeing with her own eyes that he is in jail. She has become less of a character and more of an agent of punishment, inflicting the curse of technology on a powerless victim. The focus of the novel is no longer personal betrayal or individuals harming other individuals; it is the great collective experiment we are unwittingly running, in turning over every detail of our lives to tech and leaving ourselves vulnerable to all manner of unanticipated attacks. Not everyone will suffer the worst consequences, and it may not matter if those who do did anything particularly wrong. As Kate remarks in the prison visiting room, “Everyone in here is innocent.”

This novel highlights the growing societal anxiety regarding the loss of privacy in an age where personal data is easily harvested and commodified for entertainment. results.title: Congress hasn't passed AI rules for schools. So these 98 teens did it themselves
results.author: Cory Turner
results.content:
Adults have struggled to set rules for AI in school. These teens figured it out
BOSTON — Over the course of one frantic, late-July weekend, 98 teens representing all 50 states put their busy lives on hold to try to do something remarkable.
The students, most of them high school juniors and seniors, gathered in a precise replica of the U.S. Senate chamber and attempted what the real, adult Congress has largely failed to do: draft and pass "legislation" to help the nation's K-12 schools navigate the questions and chaos created by artificial intelligence.
Should students be allowed to use AI on assignments? What about on tests? Is it schools' job to teach the nation's children what AI is and how to use it? There is no national policy for AI use in schools, meaning states and school districts have had to scramble to craft their own.
"This is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for us to actually help and try to change the country for the better," said student Gabriel Sutphin, representing South Carolina, speaking from the chamber floor at the Edward M. Kennedy Institute for the United States Senate.
To these teens, the stakes for getting ahead of AI are clear. They pointed out how adult leaders were slow to protect students from the risks of other tech developments.
"We missed the mark with social media and phones," said Hunter Wurzel, a high school senior representing Ohio. "That's been a huge talking point already [this weekend], is how we failed to implement those things into education and teach the youth how to use them."
Wurzel and his 97 colleagues were handpicked by their school leaders and hosted by a handful of education- and tech-focused groups, including the Edward M. Kennedy Institute, AASA (The School Superintendents Association), and Day of AI, a nonprofit launched out of MIT's RAISE AI literacy initiative.
At times during the weekend, where NPR was able to watch the events unfold, the bill seemed doomed, only to be revived by a flurry of student-led negotiation, old-fashioned compromises and some spirited speeches.
"[This bill] is about who gets a seat at the table. Today, students have that seat," Bena Mejia Romero of Connecticut told her fellow senators before the final vote.
Ultimately, their Students First Act passed overwhelmingly, 82-16.
Among the bill's requirements: States should provide AI literacy as soon as students get access to classroom devices; AI use should be banned on all graded tests; and teachers can require an oral defense of any project from a student suspected of using AI inappropriately. (You can read the full bill at the end of this article.)
"The adults themselves haven't been able to come to consensus on this, right? And so now it falls to the kids. Let them lead the way," said Jeffrey Riley, the executive director of Day of AI and former education commissioner of Massachusetts.
While the Students First Act isn't actually law, any more than the teens are actually senators, AASA plans to send the text to its members: 10,000 school leaders across the country, many of whom are right now crafting their own AI rules in the absence of regulation.
Rules for students
When students arrived at the start of the weekend, they were presented with a stew of policies that they had suggested in the run-up to the event. Then they were divided into subcommittees — focused on students, educators, administrators and families — to debate the dozens of proposals and create a coherent bill they could all support.
The student-focused section of the final bill includes 15 provisions, several focused on a concern many of the senators shared: that teens are using AI to do their thinking for them.
Without guidance and guardrails, "[AI use] is just gonna go unhinged," said Campbell McHenry, a high school junior from Mississippi. "Everyone's gonna stop learning and start relying on AI. Instead of using it as a tool, they're gonna use it as a brain."
Among the bill's student-focused proposals:
- Approved uses: Students should not be allowed to use AI for writing, "though editing, brainstorming and studying" with AI should be allowed after eighth grade.
- Prove mastery: Students permitted to use AI should have to cite how they used it and demonstrate their grasp of a subject through discussions, handwritten tests or oral defenses.
- Plagiarism review: Any student suspected of using AI inappropriately should have their work reviewed not just by AI checker software, which can be unreliable, but also two school officials. 
One of the most contentious issues was deciding when students should first be exposed to AI in the classroom: High school? Middle school? Earlier?
Lucia Herrera, a Missouri high schooler, took issue with an early draft of the bill.
"There's nothing that says students need to be proficient before using it," Herrera told her subcommittee colleagues. "It's basically saying they can use it whenever. Which I think is a misuse of it."
Her subcommittee's proposed solution: require schools to teach AI literacy as soon as devices are introduced in the classroom, including misinformation, plagiarism, bias in AI design, student privacy, appropriate academic use and AI's environmental impact.
When the provision came up later that day, before the full Senate, Connecticut's Bena Mejia Romero told her fellow student lawmakers they should support the new requirement. "If we're going to be using devices, we should know the dangers and the benefits that they have."
But one of the senators from California, Om Lala, argued that requiring schools to begin teaching AI literacy would be a heavy lift. "Teachers already are pretty under-resourced."
Tristan Tjetjep of Tennessee added that he worried how "underprivileged schools" would pay for this new instruction.
Suddenly, the students had run headlong into U.S. schools' funding inequities — a problem they attempted to resolve with a requirement that the federal government chip in funding.
Rules for educators, parents and caregivers
The Students First Act not only covers students' use of AI but also insists on rules for educators:
- Approved teacher use of AI: Allowed for tasks including lesson planning, making practice materials, providing feedback and improving instruction.
- Must have a clear AI policy: Each semester, teachers need to post "a clear, written AI usage policy," explaining when AI is allowed and when it's not. 
What's more, if an AI detector flags potential inappropriate AI use in a student paper, the bill says "teachers must personally investigate the issue before reporting the student to admin."
The student senators struggled with the 10 provisions in the bill's parents/guardians section because, as Isabella Stringer of New Hampshire said on the Senate floor, "We cannot legislate parenthood. Schools cannot tell parents what or how to teach your children."
As such, some of the provisions here suggest rather than tell. For instance, one says simply that parents should encourage balanced technology habits and emphasize the importance of ethical academic behavior at home.
The early version of the bill also gave parents a full veto over their students' AI access, but many of the senators argued that AI is here to stay and students must be taught how to use it.
"Giving [parents] the complete say, especially in middle to high school, in what their child can and can't do with AI is gonna limit [students] because a lot of [adults] don't even know what AI is themselves," said junior Tatiyana Reaves of North Carolina.
In one of the weekend's more passionate exchanges, senators debated what should happen if a student attempts to use a school-based AI tool, like a chatbot, "for emotional support."
Several teens worried that if a student confided sensitive information about, say, their sexuality or a mental health crisis, they should be able to trust that it would be kept private.
But Dylan Dornack of Iowa argued on the Senate floor that, for students in crisis or experiencing suicidal thoughts, the technology must alert a human.
"This could be lifesaving," Dornack told his colleagues, "whether or not that student is fearful that they might get outed. This is just one of those things that has to be taken to trusted adults."
Ultimately, the students agreed: When a school chatbot detects a student in need of emotional support, it should not fulfill the student's request but instead alert school officials.
The rush to passage
At the end of the whirlwind weekend, the student senators gathered in the replica chamber and more than half volunteered to address their colleagues for one minute each.
Dornack was the first to speak and called the bill an important, if imperfect, foundation for schools' AI policies. "You have to lay the blocks before you can have the building. So here I say, let's lay the blocks and let's pass this."
But Jadelynn Petitjean of Alabama called the bill an "unstable foundation" and opposed it.
Earlier in the day, West Virginia's Ethan Liu had also opposed it, highlighting several contradictions in the bill, including amendments that both restricted students' AI access while appearing to give teachers wide discretion over when and how AI is used.
"I thought it reflected really badly on us. I had a whole different speech planned out against this bill, actually. It was really good," Liu told the Senate chamber before the final vote.
But at the last minute, the event's organizers allowed the students to iron out a few of the bill's inconsistencies, and, as a result, Liu changed his vote, saying "this bill is in much better shape."
Student after student walked to the microphone at the front of the chamber, and most endorsed the bill, including Kendall Terao-Toma of Hawaii:
"This is for our future — not just for education but for the workforce we will join, the economy that we will build and the communities we will lead."
Edited by: Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen; audio story produced by: Lauren Migaki
Visual design and development by: LA Johnson

Ninety-eight high school students from across the United States gathered in Boston to draft and pass the "Students First Act," a comprehensive policy framework for artificial intelligence in schools.

### Key Points
- The student-led simulation took place at the Edward M. Kennedy Institute for the United States Senate, hosted by groups including AASA and MIT’s Day of AI.
- The "Students First Act" passed with an 82-16 vote, establishing guidelines for AI literacy, classroom usage, and academic integrity.
- Key provisions include banning AI on graded tests, requiring oral defenses for suspected plagiarism, and mandating that school chatbots alert officials to student crises.
- AASA, The School Superintendents Association, plans to distribute the bill’s text to 10,000 school leaders nationwide to assist in developing local AI policies.

### Why it Matters
This initiative provides a rare, student-centered perspective on technology regulation that addresses the current policy vacuum in American K-12 education. By offering a concrete framework, these students are influencing how school districts nationwide might balance the educational benefits of AI with the need for academic guardrails.

results.title: Trump Accounts And The Two Economies
results.author:
Bob Burgin, Forbes Books Author, 
 Bob Burgin, Forbes Books Author
 https://www.forbes.com/sites/forbesbooksauthors/people/bobburgin/
results.content:
For about forty years, America has been splitting into two economies. In one, you own things that compound — equity, a stake in the companies doing the work, wealth that grows while you sleep. In the other, you own only your time, and you sell it by the hour. For a generation, the first economy has pulled away from the second: the wealthiest 10 percent of households now own about 90 percent of the stock market, while the bottom half own barely 1 percent. Artificial intelligence will eventually turn that gap into a canyon.
The accounts that launched this month are the first serious attempt to build a bridge across it. And, sensibly, they start with children.
Earlier this month, the President rang the opening bells of the New York Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq from the Oval Office, marking the launch of Invest America — the initiative the administration has branded Trump Accounts, an investment account for every American child, federally seeded for some, and creating a vehicle for the wealthy to contribute at scale. The name is in the title because it’s what you’ve heard this called; now set it aside. It invites you to file the idea under a political debate before you’ve understood it, and what sits underneath is far bigger than politics.
One of the primary men behind that opening door is Brad Gerstner, founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, who has pushed the idea since 2020. Its origin is a kitchen table: Gerstner had opened accounts for his two sons at birth, and one of them, Lincoln, asked the question that became national policy — Well, this doesn’t seem fair. Why do we get these, and what about the other kids? Every American child, all 70 million of them, is now eligible to open an account and potentially own a slice of the country’s capital markets.
The Divide
Lincoln’s question is the whole thing in miniature: some children are born onto the compounding side of the economy, and most are not.
Look at where a generation of growth actually went. Over the same decades that stock prices soared, wages lagged far behind. This isn’t a forecast or a theory — it’s the documented record of the last forty years, and nobody serious disputes it. If you owned the compounding side, you pulled away. If you owned only your hours, you stayed roughly in place or fell further behind.
Why AI Widens It
I wrote a book called Emergence about how our brains, constrained to about 20 watts of power, built intelligence beyond biology, and what happens now that we’ve plugged intelligence into the power grid. One of the things we explore together in the book is the AI trajectory, which, if you follow far enough into the future, stops being a story about machines and becomes a story about which side of this divide you’re on.
Here is the part that gets misunderstood. In the short and medium term, AI is likely to create more jobs than it destroys. Some jobs will go away fast — a call-center representative, for one — but on the whole, job growth could continue for a decade or more. When the cost of producing something collapses, its price falls, and it becomes cheaper, unlocking demand that never would have been penciled out before. I watched a version of this firsthand back in the 1980s, when, as a college student, I rebuilt a real estate firm’s giant paper spreadsheets in a new program called Lotus 1-2-3. Some accounting jobs got cut, and yet the field grew to a record 1.6 million today. Spreadsheets didn’t end accounting jobs; they multiplied the analysts. After the ATM, teller jobs rose for two decades because cheaper branches meant more could be opened — until a different technology, online banking, finally shrank them.
But more jobs is not the same as a smaller divide. Even in the optimistic case, AI does one thing relentlessly: it makes capital more productive than labor. The returns flow to whoever owns the machines, the models, the companies. So paychecks can hold — even grow — while the gap between the two economies keeps widening, because the compounding is happening on a side most people don’t reach. And as AI becomes embodied, carried into the physical world by robots, even expanding demand may not be enough to keep every worker on the labor side employed. The kind of reversal online banking eventually brought to tellers could potentially arrive across the economy. The gap becomes an uncrossable canyon.
This is Not Politics
There are two familiar answers to a widening divide, and both are incomplete.
The left says redistribute income from the capital side to the labor side through the government with a larger safety net and programs, welfare by another name, run through a government that has proven incompetent at exactly this. And worse, that leaves people where they are, on the shrinking side, but even more dependent on government. The right says let the market run. But the market, left to its own devices, has left most people on the side that is falling behind.
There is a third way that combines the left’s diagnostic focus with the right’s powerful tools. Capital is winning — so put people on the side of capital. Don’t redistribute income; that is a known failed model. The framework is not safety nets. It is ownership pathways.
That is not only a change of policy; it is a change of language. For a century, we have described the people who fall behind in the vocabulary of the welfare state — benefits, handouts, entitlements. This is the language of a failing welfare state. Ownership speaks and thinks differently. Make people owners and watch what happens. Owners have a completely different view of those who build wealth when they participate in the journey: Gratitude.
The First Bridge
That is what these accounts actually are — they are not just a savings program, but the first serious mechanism to move ordinary people onto the compounding side of the economy, built while the already large divide is still narrow enough to cross and early enough in a wave of vast wealth creation that new owners can ride the wave up.
We know the shape of the model works because it has been partly proven at a smaller scale. Alaska took the wealth from the Trans-Alaska Pipeline and made every resident an owner; the Permanent Fund has paid each Alaskan a dividend for four decades. It is not welfare. It is a return on ownership. Norway did the same with North Sea oil. Both have their flaws, but both turned a windfall into citizen ownership rather than a bureaucratic welfare model, and both laid real groundwork here.
The honest danger is the years in between. A $1,000 seed today is not a stake that can catch a worker displaced tomorrow; the bridge has to be built faster than the canyon widens. That is the real race, and it is the reason to start now rather than once the crossing is already too wide.
And notice who is funding it. The money is pouring in — $6.25 billion from Michael and Susan Dell late last year, entire states adopted by Ray Dalio and by Gerstner himself, two million children handed SpaceX shares by Gwynne Shotwell — with Gerstner projecting more than $100 billion in private contributions within a year. The same capital that calculates its way out of high-tax states is sprinting to put money directly into children’s ownership. It was never unwilling to give; it was unwilling to give to a middleman it didn’t trust. Design a direct path onto the capital side, and the wallet opens. When the app went live, it hit No. 1 in the App Store’s finance category and rose into the top five overall, behind ChatGPT and Claude — tens of millions of families not so much signing up for a benefit, but rather being let in.
Expanding the Bridge to All Americans
The honest question is how you fund a crossing for all Americans, and the answer follows the same logic: you build the bridge from the side of the river that is rising.
The old economy taxes labor — a system designed to take a share of wages. But wages are potentially the shrinking side in a longer AI trajectory. The growing side is capital and corporate profit, and AI pours fuel on exactly that: As it makes companies radically more efficient and more profitable, their earnings climb, and the taxes those earnings generate climb with them. This is not a new entitlement funded by the old economy. It is a claim on the new one, helping people to become owners. A free-market model for shrinking the divide.
There is a much bigger source hiding in plain sight, and it may be the one that finally breaks the partisan logjam. Every dollar lost to government waste, fraud, and excessive spending is potentially a dollar of ownership the public never receives.
Today, cutting that waste is a bloodless austerity fight nobody wins, because the savings just vanish back into the general fund. But imagine the dollars reclaimed were converted, pro rata, into ownership stakes for citizens. You would see far less irrational resistance to government efforts to curb waste, fraud, and excessive spending.
And here is the quiet elegance. The wealthy already carry most of the load; the top 10% pay roughly 70% of all federal income taxes. But an ownership dividend would be split pro rata: one equal share per citizen, never doled out by need. Even Michael Dell would get a slice — far smaller than he paid in, and a tiny fraction of what he already donated to these very accounts for children. Listen differently when you hear “tax the rich their fair share.” In this model, the money quietly runs downhill, across the divide, without the perverse incentives of inefficient tax increases routing money through the most inefficient mechanism possible, the government.
That is why starting with children is smart. It is the politically possible first span, and the place where compounding has the most time to work. Build the rails for kids now, while the crossing is short and the compounding window is long, then widen them, over time, toward every American through naturally compounding increased tax revenue and radical reduction in government spending, waste, and fraud.
The Bridge Before the Canyon
A dividend funded to citizen-owners isn’t exactly altruistic. It is self-preserving at scale. It is the spark plug that keeps the engine firing. If AI produces everything and most people own nothing, buying stops, and the whole machine stalls. Ownership keeps money in motion by keeping people on the right side of the divide.
I grew up in my early years in government-subsidized housing and in poverty, and over fifty years, I clawed my way from one side of this divide to the other. I have the view from both. Brad Gerstner and this administration have now built the mechanism, and my optimism about the country’s future has risen as a result. What we owe each other now is the conversation about what it is for: ownership over dependency. Participation in the extraordinary American capital markets.
And right now, the wealthy finally have a direct, efficient way to help build it. And they are now and will continue. Where I grew up in Texas, we had a saying for the skeptics in a moment like this.
“Hide and watch.”

The new Invest America initiative, branded as Trump Accounts, aims to bridge the national wealth gap by providing every American child with an investment account to foster capital ownership.

### Key Points
- The program allows all 70 million American children to open investment accounts, with federal seeding for some and private contributions for others.
- Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, a primary architect of the initiative, projects over $100 billion in private funding within the first year.
- Major donors include Michael and Susan Dell, Ray Dalio, and SpaceX, with two million children already receiving shares in the latter.
- The initiative seeks to move citizens from a labor-based economy to a capital-based one, countering the wealth-concentrating effects of artificial intelligence.
- The model draws inspiration from the Alaska Permanent Fund and Norway’s sovereign wealth fund, which distribute dividends to residents based on resource ownership.

### Why it Matters
This initiative represents a shift from traditional welfare-based redistribution toward an ownership-focused model designed to mitigate the economic divide exacerbated by AI. By integrating citizens into capital markets, the program aims to ensure long-term economic participation and stability as automation increases the productivity of capital relative to labor.

results.title: The new Washington bar exam could not demonstrate minimum technical competence
results.author: Jason Weisberger
results.content:
In what seems like a story from the late 1990s, and not 2026, Washington's bar-licensure task force wanted to wait until 2027 to give their new high-tech exam time to "work out any issues with its administration." The state Supreme Court chose 2026. You know what happened next…
Roughly 645 aspiring lawyers couldn't get their laptops to connect to the Wi-Fi or do whatever the National Conference of Bar Examiners software was supposed to do. The bar exam had to be canceled, sending their budding careers into turmoil.
Recent law school graduates spend months studying for the bar exam. They often spend thousands of dollars, too, paying for test prep materials, travel, lodging, childcare, and other costs in order to sit for the multiday ordeal that their job prospects depend on. They forgo personal obligations and rearrange their lives because their livelihoods are at stake.
They should not have to live like this. And Washington has recognized for years that it doesn't need to make them do so. In July 2020, for instance, when the COVID-19 pandemic made it too dangerous to administer the bar exam, the state supreme court issued a one-time grant of "diploma privilege." This allowed graduates of accredited law schools who were applying for bar admission at that time to become licensed attorneys without taking the exam.
By Wednesday afternoon, the deans of all three law schools in Washington sent letters to the state supreme court urging it to grant diploma privilege to those affected by Tuesday's fiasco. "Diploma privilege presents—by far—the most equitable remedy," said Anthony Varona, dean of Seattle University School of Law. Tamara Lawson, dean of University of Washington Law School, similarly identified diploma privilege as "the only equitable remedy" that would make sure "the financial, professional, and emotional burdens of this catastrophic failure are not shifted to the test takers."
Balls and Strikes
"Ready for launch" met the Yakima Convention Center.
Previously:
• ChatGPT not that great at bar exam after all
• Remote bar exams for aspiring attorneys are a terrible and dangerous idea
results.summary:
Washington’s state bar exam was canceled after software failures prevented approximately 645 aspiring lawyers from accessing the required testing platform at the Yakima Convention Center on Tuesday.

### Key Points
- Technical issues with the National Conference of Bar Examiners software caused widespread connectivity failures during the exam.
- The Washington State Supreme Court mandated the 2026 testing date despite a task force recommendation to delay implementation until 2027.
- Deans from Seattle University, the University of Washington, and Gonzaga University are formally requesting "diploma privilege" for all affected candidates.
- Diploma privilege would allow qualified law school graduates to obtain licensure without retaking the high-stakes examination.
- Affected candidates face significant financial and professional setbacks due to the costs of test preparation and lost employment opportunities.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the systemic risks associated with relying on centralized, high-tech testing platforms for critical professional licensing requirements. Granting diploma privilege would set a significant precedent for how states handle administrative failures that jeopardize the livelihoods of thousands of legal professionals.

results.title: Nearly 3,000 heat-related deaths during summer heatwaves, UKHSA estimates
results.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
results.content:
- Published
England is on track this year for the highest number of heat-related deaths since records began, according to estimates by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).
In a preliminary assessment, it said there were an estimated 2,877 heat-related deaths during the May and June heatwaves, almost double the figure for the whole of last year.
An estimated 753 deaths were associated with the 24-27 May heatwave and a further 2,124 with the one from 21-28 June. Definitive figures are expected in early 2027.
Both spells broke Met Office UK monthly temperature records, with 35.1C (95.2F) recorded at Kew Gardens on 26 May and 38.0C recorded at Lingwood, Norfolk on 26 June.
The current record for heat-related deaths was set in 2022, when 2,985 deaths were recorded.
Report author Dr Ross Thompson, from the UKHSA, said "while the figures are interim, they suggest that, if we experience more periods of hot weather this summer, we could see the highest number of heat-associated deaths on record".
Thompson added: "These figures highlight the significant danger that very hot weather can pose to people's health.
"This is particularly true for those who are more vulnerable including older adults and people with underlying medical conditions."
He said "as the climate becomes warmer, we can expect periods of hot weather to become longer, more frequent and more extreme", adding that it is vital the country is prepared to deal with higher temperatures.
Earlier this week parts of the UK sweltered through another heatwave that peaked on Wednesday, with temperature reaching 35.2C in Writtle, Essex.
Cooler conditions and some rain are on the way for some on Thursday and into the weekend, but likely not in the driest areas.
On Wednesday drought was declared across more than half of England due to hot, dry weather taking its toll on the country's water supplies.
The Environment Agency (EA) said the drought covers much of central, eastern and southern England, with director of water Helen Wakeham saying the weather "means we are currently using water faster than nature can replenish it".
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the sweltering heat has had a "serious impact this summer on people's health and on our NHS".
She added: "My thoughts are with all those who have lost loved ones as a result of the long and intense heatwaves in recent months.
"And my heartfelt thanks go to the NHS staff, care workers and emergency responders who have worked tirelessly through these exceptionally busy and challenging months to protect and care for people affected by the heat."
May's heatwave smashed the temperature record for that month, with a high of 35.1C recorded at Kew Gardens. It surpassed the previous high of 32.8C set back in 1922 and equalled in 1944.
A month later, June's heatwave set another monthly temperature record - 38.0C in Lingwood, Norfolk. The previous high was 35.6C set in 1957 and equalled during the infamous 1976 heatwave.
Both were caused by a "heat dome" - a stalled area of high pressure that trapped hot air over the region.
It is not just the UK that has dealt with sweltering temperatures this summer, as much of western Europe has also faced record-breaking temperatures.
In the last week deadly wildfires have hit parts of France, Spain and Greece - with tens of thousands of people forced to evacuate their homes.
results.summary:
England is on track to record its highest number of heat-related deaths this year, with the UK Health Security Agency estimating 2,877 fatalities during May and June heatwaves.

### Key Points
- The UK Health Security Agency estimates 2,877 heat-related deaths occurred during May and June, nearly doubling the total recorded for all of 2022.
- Record-breaking temperatures reached 35.1C at Kew Gardens in May and 38.0C in Lingwood, Norfolk, during June.
- Both heatwaves were driven by a "heat dome," a stalled high-pressure system that trapped hot air over the region.
- The Environment Agency declared a drought across more than half of England as water consumption outpaces natural replenishment.
- Definitive mortality figures for the year are not expected to be finalized until early 2027.

### Why it Matters
These record-breaking figures underscore the growing public health risks posed by increasingly frequent and extreme heat events linked to a warming climate. The strain on the NHS and the declaration of widespread drought highlight the urgent need for improved national infrastructure and preparedness strategies to protect vulnerable populations.
